For the DRC, this suggests that the feasibility of maintaining regular collections should form part of surveillance planning alongside the geographical distribution of sites.

Ultimately, the most appropriate network configuration may not be the one containing the largest number of sites, but the configuration that achieves an acceptable balance between surveillance objectives, environmental representation, geographical coverage and sustainable operational requirements.

## Strengths and limitations

A principal strength of this study is the comparison of three successive national sentinel-network configurations using a consistent geospatial modelling framework. Applying the same walking and motorised friction surfaces across configurations enabled differences associated with network arrangements to be examined without introducing variation arising from different transport datasets.

The analysis also distinguished between travel from DPS offices to their administratively assigned sentinel sites and national geographical accessibility to the nearest DPS office or sentinel site. These measures capture different aspects of surveillance-network performance. In addition, the walking-route analysis provided information about the geographical lengths of modelled journeys beyond travel-time estimates alone.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings.

First, the MAP 2020 friction surfaces were applied to all three configurations. The comparisons therefore do not reconstruct historical travel conditions between 2003–2005, 2014 and 2021. Changes in modelled accessibility reflect differences in the network configurations rather than observed improvements or deterioration in transport infrastructure over time.

Second, modelled travel times were not validated against actual field journeys. The friction surfaces do not explicitly account for ferry waiting times, boat schedules, overnight stays, temporary road closures, seasonal flooding, insecurity or the availability of transport at the time of travel. Consequently, the estimated times represent potential accessibility under model assumptions rather than verified operational journey durations.

Third, geographical precision varied across DPS and sentinel-site locations. Some coordinates represented settlements or administrative seats rather than exact facility entrances. Eight established DPS-to-site pairs had identical analytical coordinates without documented independent replacement coordinates, and an additional identical pair occurred in the proposed 2021 network. These uncertainties may affect the interpretation of short journeys and geographical co-location.

Fourth, national coverage was measured as the percentage of modelled land area within selected travel-time thresholds. The analysis did not estimate population-weighted accessibility or incorporate geographical variation in malaria burden, vector abundance or ecological suitability. Therefore, the results cannot determine what proportion of the population was covered by the network or whether sentinel sites adequately represented malaria-vector populations across different environments.

Fifth, the analysis did not measure surveillance costs, actual sampling frequency, laboratory capacity, staff availability or the likelihood that planned supervisory visits would be completed. These factors are necessary for a comprehensive evaluation of operational feasibility.

Finally, the proposed 2021 configuration included 51 of the 52 planned sites because the additional location in Kasaï-Central could not be reliably identified. The results therefore describe the geographically identifiable proposed configuration rather than the complete intended expansion. In addition, the analysis evaluated proposed locations and did not establish whether every additional site had become operational.

These limitations do not invalidate the observed geographical differences between network configurations, but they restrict the extent to which modelled accessibility can be interpreted as actual surveillance performance.

## Future research

Future work should assess whether the geographical expansion of the sentinel network also improves its ecological and epidemiological representativeness. Integrating environmental covariates, predicted malaria-vector distributions and malaria burden could help identify areas and vector habitats that remain inadequately represented by existing and proposed surveillance locations.

An important next step is to validate modelled accessibility against observed supervisory journeys, accounting for seasonal transport conditions, river crossings and operational delays. Independently verified coordinates for DPS offices and sentinel facilities would improve the accuracy of these comparisons.

Building on these findings, spatial optimisation approaches could be used to evaluate alternative sentinel-network configurations under realistic constraints on travel time, sampling frequency and available resources. This would help identify surveillance arrangements that balance geographical coverage with operational feasibility and scientific objectives.

# Conclusion

The expansion of the Democratic Republic of the Congo's malaria sentinel surveillance network substantially improved modelled geographical accessibility. The proportion of national land area within 24 hours of walking travel from the nearest sentinel site increased from 10.3% under the historical 11-site network to 38.4% under the proposed 51-site configuration, while six-hour motorised coverage increased from 31.2% to 61.2%. However, the proposed additional sites generally required longer journeys from their assigned Provincial Health Division offices, highlighting potential logistical challenges associated with network expansion.

These findings demonstrate that increasing the number of sentinel sites can reduce geographical coverage gaps but does not necessarily ensure operational accessibility or sustained surveillance. Future network planning should therefore consider the trade-off between extending geographical coverage and maintaining a surveillance system that can be supported and operated consistently.

## Supplementary Table S2: Full national sentinel-site accessibility

```{r}
#| label: tbl-full-coverage
#| tbl-cap: "Area-weighted percentage of the DRC within each modelled travel-time threshold of the nearest sentinel site."

full_coverage <- coverage |>
  mutate(
    Mode = if_else(
      mode == "walking",
      "Walking",
      "Motorised"
    ),
    `Threshold (h)` = threshold_hours,
    `Accessible area (%)` = round(
      percent_modelled_area,
      1
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    Mode,
    network,
    `Threshold (h)`,
    `Accessible area (%)`
  ) |>
  arrange(
    Mode,
    `Threshold (h)`,
    network
  )

knitr::kable(
  full_coverage,
  align = "lcrc"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-site-level

    `DPS office` = dps_office,
    `Sentinel site` = sentinel_site,
    `Straight km` = round(straight_km, 1),

      walking_route_km, 1
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(
    Province,
    `Sentinel site`
  )

knitr::kable(
  site_table,
  align = "llllrrrr"
)
```

## Supplementary note: Reproducibility and quality control

Ten accessibility rasters were validated, comprising four nearest-DPS surfaces (two networks × two travel modes) and six nearest-sentinel surfaces (three networks × two travel modes). All source locations returned zero travel time at their corresponding raster origins, and no missing origin values were identified.

The assigned travel-time analysis generated 176 network-scenario records. The walking-route dataset included all 88 walking scenario records and 52 unique coordinate pairs.

The saved walking-route travel times were compared with the current assigned-journey calculations. All 88 records matched, with no missing route distances and a maximum difference of approximately 2.9 minutes, consistent with the precision of previously saved travel times.

The computational workflow comprises the seven numbered scripts `00_packages.R` to `06_run_analysis.R`. The software environment was recorded in `output/unified/R_session_information.txt`, and the model configuration in `output/unified/accessibility_model_configuration.csv`.

A complete reconstruction requires the original coordinate datasets, geographical boundaries, MAP friction surfaces and access to the relevant R packages. The modelling outputs were retained to allow computational checks without repeatedly rebuilding expensive transition matrices.
